title: Two kitchens, one pantry

beats.say: Why would one company keep the same trip data in two different places? Because two teams asked, and each wanted the data in its own home.

show.sub: Why teams end up with two platforms

beats.say: Picture a restaurant with two kitchens. Data scientists cook in one, called Databricks. Finance cooks in the other, called Snowflake. Both need the same ingredients, which here are trip records.
The easy fix is to buy ingredients twice. But now you have two delivery crews, two grocery bills, and two stock lists that slowly disagree. Which one is right?
The better idea is one shared pantry. Keep a single copy of the table, and let each kitchen read from it.

check.q: Why is copying the trip tables into both platforms a poor default?
opts: It doubles pipelines and bills, and the copies can disagree
It makes queries run slower in both platforms
Neither platform can store trip data
check.why: Two copies need two loading pipelines and two bills, and any delay or bug lets them drift into two versions of the truth.

work: List which tables are already copied into more than one platform.
Ask each team why it needs its own copy before agreeing to build another pipeline.

title: What doubles, and how one table fixes it

beats.say: If you copy a trip table into both platforms, what exactly doubles?

show.sub: Copy a trip table into two platforms

beats.say: Nearly everything. Say the table is two terabytes. Two copies means four terabytes stored, two pipelines to load it, and two compute bills. Each platform also answers the same four questions: how it stores data, how it skips data, what it costs, and how you govern it.

The way out is an open table format. The data sits once as Parquet files in cloud storage, with a metadata layer listing which files belong to the table. Databricks writes it as Delta, and can publish Iceberg metadata beside it. Snowflake reads that as an Iceberg table.
So two engines, one set of files, and one truth.

show.title: The shared-table idea
items: Each engine brings its own compute

check.q: What makes one table readable by both Databricks and Snowflake?
opts: Both platforms copy it nightly into their own format
Data lives once in open files, with table metadata both engines understand
Snowflake runs inside Databricks
check.why: An open table format keeps one set of Parquet files plus metadata, so each engine reads the same data with its own compute.

work: Check which of your tables already use Delta or Iceberg.
Estimate storage plus pipeline cost for a table you currently copy.

title: Where a shared table bites

beats.say: If both platforms read one table, who is allowed to write to it?
Usually just one. Two writers committing to the same table at once can fight over its history and break it. So pick one owner, say Databricks, and make Snowflake read only.

Next gotcha is metadata lag. Snowflake reads a snapshot of the table's file list. If that snapshot has not refreshed, finance sees yesterday's trips while data scientists see today's. Know your refresh interval.

show.title: Stale snapshot
items: Reader still holds the old file list

beats.say: Last, governance does not travel. A mask on the driver phone column in one platform is not enforced when the other reads the raw files. Apply rules where each engine reads, or restrict direct access to storage.

check.q: Finance in Snowflake reports fewer trips than the data scientists in Databricks on the same table. What is the most likely cause?
opts: Snowflake is reading an older metadata snapshot
Parquet drops rows when shared
Databricks counts trips twice
check.why: Readers see the table as of the last metadata they loaded. Until it refreshes, newly committed files are invisible to them.

work: Name a single owner platform for each shared table.
Document the metadata refresh interval and show it to report users.
Review column masks and row filters for every table exposed to both engines.

title: When two platforms are the wrong call

beats.say: When is running two platforms the wrong answer?
When the split is political, not technical. Two platforms mean two skill sets, two security models, and cross-platform reads that can cost network egress if storage sits in another cloud or region.

show.title: Hidden costs of two
items: Two skill sets to hire and train
Two security models to keep aligned
Egress fees when storage is far away

beats.say: Choose one platform if the table is small and one team does most of the work. Keep both when machine learning and finance reporting truly need different engines, and share one table between them.
Decide by measuring: who queries it, how often, and what a copy costs each month. Then pick the cheapest design that keeps one truth.

show.title: Decision inputs
items: Monthly cost of a copy versus a shared read

check.q: Which situation best justifies keeping both platforms on one shared table?
opts: Both teams just prefer their own tool and the table is tiny
ML work and finance reporting each need a different engine on the same data
The company wants two independent versions of the data
check.why: A genuine workload difference justifies two engines. Sharing one table then avoids duplicate storage, pipelines and drift.

work: Write down the real workload reason each team needs its platform.
Price egress for any cross-region or cross-cloud shared reads before committing.

title: Minibus or hired car

beats.say: Why would the same overnight job cost less on a computer that lives for only twenty minutes?

Think of transport. An all-purpose cluster is a shared minibus. It stays parked with the engine running, so analysts can hop on any time to use notebooks. That is handy, but you pay while it sits idle.
A job cluster is a hired car for one trip. It appears when the scheduled job starts, drives the route, and disappears. It also has a lower rate per hour.
So the rule is simple. Exploring by hand, use the minibus. Scheduled work, hire the car. You stop paying the moment the trip ends.

check.q: A nightly ETL job runs for about 25 minutes. Where should it run?
opts: On a job cluster created for the run and ended after it
On the shared all-purpose cluster so it is already warm
On a SQL warehouse because the job is on a schedule
On a larger all-purpose cluster that stays up all night
check.why: Scheduled work belongs on job clusters. They exist only for the run and are billed at a lower rate, so you pay nothing while idle.

work: List your scheduled jobs and check which still run on all-purpose clusters.
Move one nightly job to a job cluster and compare the next bill.

title: Two lines on every bill

beats.say: A two hour job produced a bill with two separate lines. What are they?
Databricks charges in DBUs, a unit of processing capability per hour. Bigger machines burn more DBUs, and the type of workload sets the price of each one.
Say a cluster burns ten DBUs an hour for two hours. That is twenty DBUs. At an example rate of fifteen cents each, Databricks bills three dollars.
Your cloud provider bills the virtual machines separately. Say five dollars an hour, so ten dollars. The total is thirteen dollars.
To control it, use cluster policies, auto termination, autoscaling, job clusters, and the billing system tables to see who spent what.

check.q: What makes up the cost of a Databricks job?
opts: DBUs times the DBU rate, plus the cloud charge for the VMs
DBUs times the DBU rate, with VMs included in that rate
The cloud charge for the VMs, with DBUs only for SQL
A flat fee per cluster, regardless of its run time
check.why: Two bills arrive: Databricks charges DBUs at a rate set by compute type, and the cloud provider separately charges for the virtual machines.

work: Query the billing system tables and rank clusters by DBUs last month.
Write a cluster policy with a maximum size and an auto termination time.

title: Auto Loader loads each file once

beats.say: A bucket receives thousands of new JSON files an hour. How do you load only the new ones, and never load one twice?
Auto Loader watches the folder and records every file it has processed. On each run it picks up only files not yet recorded, so a restart does not duplicate data.
It also infers the schema from the files and stores it at the schema location you give it. When new fields appear, it can evolve the schema instead of crashing.
Values that do not fit, like text in a number column, go to a rescued data column. Nothing is silently lost, and you can inspect it later.

check.q: A new file arrives with a text value in a column typed as a number. What does Auto Loader do?
opts: Puts the value in the rescued data column and keeps loading
Drops the whole file and keeps no record of the problem
Stops the stream until someone fixes the schema by hand
Converts the text to zero so the column type stays valid
check.why: Data that does not fit the schema goes to the rescued data column, so the load continues and the odd value can be inspected later.

work: Check that every Auto Loader stream has its own schema location.
Add a daily check that counts non-empty rescued data rows.

title: Declare tables, skip the plumbing

beats.say: What if you wrote only the query for each table, and the platform handled order, retries and servers?

That is declarative pipelines, long called Delta Live Tables. You declare each table as a query. The platform reads them, works out which depends on which, and runs them in order, processing only new data.
You attach expectations, which are data quality rules. A rule can warn and keep the row, drop the bad rows, or fail the whole update. Pick by how costly bad data is.

chip.text: Choose by cost of bad data

beats.say: It can also apply a change feed as a Type 1 or Type 2 dimension in one statement. That replaces the hand written merge, which is easy to get subtly wrong.

check.q: You want bad rows removed but the pipeline kept running. What do you set on the expectation?
opts: Drop the rows that fail and let the update continue
Warn only, which removes the rows and keeps running
Fail the update, which deletes bad rows and restarts
Nothing, because the platform cleans bad rows itself
check.why: Expectations can warn and keep rows, drop failing rows and continue, or fail the update. Only the drop mode removes bad rows and carries on.

work: Pick one hand-written merge and test replacing it with the built-in change feed statement.
Add a drop expectation on a key column and track how many rows it removes.

title: Photon is not liquid clustering

beats.say: Photon or liquid clustering: which makes queries faster? Why is that a trick question?
Photon is an execution engine. It is vectorised, written in C plus plus, and replaces parts of Spark's Java engine for SQL and DataFrame work. It runs the same reading and computing faster.
Liquid clustering is about layout. It organises data files by chosen columns, so a query can skip files it does not need. It reduces how much gets read at all.
So they are different layers, and they stack. One speeds up the work, the other shrinks the work. Saying one replaces the other is the mistake interviewers listen for.

check.q: How do Photon and liquid clustering relate?
opts: Photon speeds query execution, clustering shrinks the data read
Both organise files, but Photon does it at query time
Clustering replaces Photon for tables with a chosen key
Photon is a layout setting that clustering later extends
check.why: Photon is a vectorised engine for how queries run. Liquid clustering lays data out so queries read fewer files. They work at different layers.

work: Run one slow query with and without Photon, and note the time.
Pick a table filtered on one column and test clustering by that column.

title: One catalog, no bypass

beats.say: Five workspaces, five sets of table permissions. How do you make one rule apply everywhere?

Unity Catalog is one catalog across all workspaces. Tables get a three level name: catalog, schema, table. It holds permissions, row filters, column masks, lineage captured from queries, and storage credentials.

Migrating an existing project has four moves. Create a metastore. Map storage through external locations. Migrate tables from the old per workspace metastore. Then replace direct storage access with grants.
That last step is the gotcha. If jobs still read the bucket directly with their own keys, they bypass every rule you just wrote.

check.q: After migrating tables to Unity Catalog, what is the biggest remaining risk?
opts: Jobs still reading storage directly, which bypasses the grants
Table names now having three levels, which breaks old queries
Lineage being lost because it is only captured by hand
Row filters applying only inside a single workspace
check.why: Grants only protect access that goes through Unity Catalog. Direct storage access with old keys skips them, so it must be replaced.

work: Search your jobs for hard-coded bucket paths and storage keys.
Map each storage path to an external location before migrating tables.

title: Matching compute to workload

beats.say: Three workloads: a nightly pipeline, a dashboard, and analysts exploring. Do they share one cluster?
Not if you care about cost. Scheduled work goes on job clusters, created per run, cheaper per hour, gone afterward. That alone removes idle spend.
Dashboards go on SQL warehouses. Serverless starts in seconds, so you avoid keeping a warehouse warm all day, but you give up some control over the machines.
Exploration is the only case for all-purpose clusters. Fence them with cluster policies, auto termination and autoscaling, and watch the billing system tables for the leaks.

check.q: Which compute choice best cuts idle spend for a scheduled pipeline?
opts: A job cluster created for each run and ended after it
A large all-purpose cluster kept running between runs
A serverless SQL warehouse kept warm all day for the job
An all-purpose cluster shared with the analyst team
check.why: Job clusters exist only for the run and cost less per hour, so there is no idle time to pay for. Shared clusters keep billing between runs.

work: Write a short rule mapping each workload type to a compute type.
Review billing system tables monthly for all-purpose clusters running pipelines.

title: Apps and agents beside the data

beats.say: An agent needs a place for approvals, a screen for humans, and a first evaluation. Do you build three separate systems?
Lakebase is managed Postgres inside the platform, with storage separate from compute. Lakehouse tables can sync into it, so an app gets fast lookups without you running a database.
Databricks Apps hosts a Python or Node web app on serverless compute, signed in with workspace identities and governed by Unity Catalog permissions. Good for an approval screen.
Agent Bricks builds a first agent from a description and your data, with an evaluation generated. Then you decide whether to hand build it.
The trade-off: these names and details change fast, and you lean harder on one vendor. Check current documentation first.

check.q: What is the main reason to try Agent Bricks before building an agent by hand?
opts: You get a first agent with an evaluation from day one
It removes the need for any evaluation of the agent later
It guarantees the agent beats a hand built framework one
It stores approvals and serves the screen for the agent
check.why: Agent Bricks gives a quick first version with a generated evaluation, so you can judge quality before deciding to hand build with the agent framework.

work: Sketch which parts of one agent need state, a screen and an evaluation.
Record the product versions you tested, since details change quickly.

title: A library with separate reading rooms

beats.say: What if a library let any number of readers use the same books without ever crowding each other?
Snowflake works like that. The books are your data, kept on shelves in cheap cloud storage, packed tightly in columns. Nobody owns the shelves.

chip.text: Data lives once, in cloud storage

beats.say: Reading rooms are virtual warehouses. Each is its own team of workers. Finance can have one for dashboards, and the nightly load can have another. They read the same books, so neither slows the other.
The front desk is cloud services. It checks who you are, knows where every book is, and plans the quickest route. Three layers, and each grows on its own.

check.q: Why can finance dashboards and the nightly load run at once without slowing each other?
opts: They run on separate warehouses reading the same stored data
Each gets its own private copy of the data
Snowflake queues the nightly load until dashboards finish
check.why: Compute is separate from storage, so each workload gets its own warehouse over one shared copy of the data.

work: Sketch which of your workloads should have their own warehouse.
Explain the three layers to a colleague in one sentence each.

title: Pruning: skipping data without indexes

beats.say: How does Snowflake find one day of data in a table of billions of rows, with no indexes?

show.sub: Billions of rows, one day wanted

beats.say: Every table is cut into micro-partitions, immutable chunks of roughly 50 to 500 megabytes uncompressed, stored by column.

For each chunk, Snowflake notes the minimum and maximum of every column. Say a query asks for the fifth of March. Any chunk whose dates run from January to the end of February cannot match, so it is never read.
That skipping is called pruning. If events arrive in date order, each chunk covers a narrow range, so a one day query might touch a few chunks out of thousands. Nothing to build, nothing to maintain.

show.title: Chunks read for a one day query

check.q: What lets Snowflake skip a micro-partition without reading it?
opts: An index you build on the column
Stored minimum and maximum values per column that rule it out
A result cache hit
check.why: Min and max metadata per column is compared with the query filter. Partitions that cannot match are pruned.

work: Check the query profile of a slow query for partitions scanned versus total.
Find a big table and note what order its data arrives in.

title: Bigger or more warehouses?

beats.say: Your query is slow. Do you buy a bigger warehouse, or more of them?
Sizes double capacity and cost at each step. Moving up a size can make one heavy query faster, for twice the credits per hour.
A multi-cluster warehouse is different. It adds copies of the same size when queries queue up. Ten analysts waiting get served at once, but one slow query is no faster.

chip.text: More at once, not faster each

beats.say: Two savers. Auto-suspend stops the warehouse when idle, and billing is per second with a one minute minimum on each start. And the result cache answers an identical query on unchanged data without waking any warehouse.

show.title: Cost savers
items: Per second billing, one minute minimum

check.q: Fifty analysts run small queries and wait in a queue. What helps most?
opts: Doubling the warehouse size
Turning on multi-cluster
Disabling auto-suspend
check.why: Queuing is a concurrency problem. Multi-cluster adds clusters for more simultaneous queries. A bigger size mainly speeds up single heavy queries.

work: Match each warehouse you run to a problem: heavy query or queuing.
Review auto-suspend timeouts against how bursty each workload is.

title: When pruning fails and clustering

beats.say: Why did a query on a ten terabyte table scan almost everything, even with a filter?

Pruning only helps when the data's order matches the filter. If rows for one customer are scattered across every micro-partition, each chunk's minimum and maximum span the whole range, and none can be skipped.

chip.text: Every range overlaps, so all are read

beats.say: The fix is a clustering key. A background service rewrites the data so similar values sit together. But it burns credits continuously as data changes.
So use it only on very large tables with selective filters that keep missing. Check the query profile first. On smaller tables, the cost beats the saving.

show.title: Cluster when
items: Pruning is poor in the profile

check.q: A medium table is queried by customer, but loaded by date, and queries are acceptably fast. What should you do?
opts: Add a clustering key right away
Leave it, since clustering costs credits and may not pay off
Build an index
check.why: Clustering is ongoing credit spend and suits very large tables with selective filters that prune badly. Snowflake has no indexes to build.

work: Pull partitions scanned versus total for your five slowest queries.
Cost a clustering key before adding one, including background credits.

title: Time Travel, Fail-safe and cloning

beats.say: Someone dropped a production table at nine this morning. Can you get it back?

Maybe, with Time Travel. Within the retention period, you can query or restore a table as it was at an earlier moment. This works because micro-partitions are immutable, so old versions simply stay around.

show.title: Time Travel
items: Old versions kept for retention period
Query or restore an earlier moment

beats.say: After retention ends, Fail-safe holds the data for a further period. But only Snowflake support can reach it, so never plan on it as your backup.

show.title: Recovery windows
items: Time Travel: you can query and restore
Neither replaces a real backup plan

beats.say: Cloning is the same trick. Create table t2 clone t1 copies only metadata. Both point at the same partitions, and you pay for storage only as they diverge. Great for test copies of production.

chip.text: Storage grows only as they diverge

check.q: What happens to storage when you clone a large table?
opts: It doubles immediately
Almost nothing at first, growing as the copies diverge
It is moved into Fail-safe
check.why: A clone copies metadata only. Both tables share the same immutable micro-partitions until changes create new ones.

work: Check the Time Travel retention set on your critical tables.
Use clones for test environments instead of copying data.

title: From landed file to fresh table

beats.say: A file lands in cloud storage. How does it become queryable rows, in minutes or even seconds?
Bulk loading uses a stage and COPY INTO. Snowpipe does it automatically when a file arrives. Snowpipe Streaming skips files and loads rows directly.
For transformations, a stream records changes since you last read it, and a task runs SQL on a schedule. Together they build incremental pipelines, but you wire and watch them yourself.
A dynamic table is simpler. You write the query and a target lag, say five minutes, and Snowflake keeps the result that fresh, incrementally where it can. It replaces most stream and task pairs.

show.title: Declare, don't wire
show.text: create dynamic table daily_sales target_lag five minutes as select ...

check.q: You want a summary table kept about five minutes fresh with the least pipeline code. What fits best?
opts: A stream and a scheduled task
A dynamic table with a target lag
COPY INTO every minute
check.why: A dynamic table is declarative. You state the query and lag, and Snowflake maintains it, incrementally where possible.

work: List your stream and task pairs and see which could be dynamic tables.
Decide which feeds need Snowpipe rather than scheduled bulk loads.

title: Evolving events with VARIANT

beats.say: Your event payload gains new fields every month. Do you alter the table every time?
Not if you land the raw payload in a VARIANT column. It holds semi-structured data, which you query with path notation and flatten into rows. New fields need no change at all.

chip.text: New fields need no schema change

beats.say: Then promote the stable fields to typed columns in a view or downstream model. You get flexibility at the edge and clean types where people query.
The trade-off: VARIANT fields often prune and compress worse than typed columns, and bad data surfaces late, at query time. So keep the raw layer loose, and the served layer strict.

show.title: Trade-offs
items: Con: errors appear at query time

check.q: What is the sound design for fast-changing event attributes?
opts: Alter the table for every new field
Land the payload in VARIANT and promote stable fields to typed columns downstream
Keep everything in VARIANT and query it directly forever
check.why: VARIANT absorbs change at the edge, while typed columns in a view or model give better performance and clear contracts for consumers.

work: Find fields in your VARIANT queries used in filters, and promote them.
Add checks on the typed layer to catch bad payloads early.

title: Controlling the Snowflake bill

beats.say: Your Snowflake bill doubled. Where do you look first?
Warehouses. Short auto-suspend saves credits. But suspend too aggressively and every restart bills a one minute minimum, so bursty workloads can cost more.
Separate workloads by warehouse so you can size and charge each one. Scale up for heavy single queries, scale out with multi-cluster for concurrency. Mixing them up wastes credits.
Then clustering. Only pay for it on huge tables with selective filters. And lean on the result cache, and on dynamic table lags no tighter than the business needs, since fresher means more compute.

show.title: Then trim
items: Relax target lag where you can

check.q: A dynamic table refreshes every minute, but the business reads it once each morning. What is the best move?
opts: Keep the lag, since fresher is always better
Raise the target lag to match real need
Cluster the table
check.why: Fresher results require more compute. Set target lag to what consumers actually need to avoid paying for freshness nobody uses.

work: Review credit use by warehouse and tie each to an owner.
Audit target lags and clustering keys against real usage.

title: One recipe book, two kitchens

beats.say: What if two restaurants could cook from one recipe book, instead of each photocopying it?
Most companies copy their data into every platform. The copies drift apart, storage costs double, and nobody knows which one is right.
Instead, keep one copy on a shared shelf, in a format both sides understand. That format is called Iceberg. It is an agreed way of labelling the files, so any engine can read them.

One rule matters. Only one cook may write in the book. Everyone else just reads. Otherwise two people edit at once and pages get mangled. And each kitchen still keeps its own lock on who may see which page.

show.title: Two house rules
items: Each kitchen keeps its own locks

check.q: Why give each shared table only one writing engine?
opts: Readers are slower than writers
Two writers can overwrite each other and mangle the table
Iceberg only supports one user
check.why: Concurrent writers through different routes cannot see each other's changes, so one can silently overwrite the other. Readers are safe because they do not change anything.

work: List the tables your two platforms both copy today and note the cost of each copy.
For each shared table, name the single engine that is allowed to write it.

title: How both engines read one table

beats.say: How can Snowflake and Databricks query the very same table without copying a byte?

The data sits as Parquet files in your own cloud bucket. Iceberg adds metadata files that list which Parquet files make up the table right now. Any engine that reads that metadata sees the same table.

chip.text: Any engine sees the same table

beats.say: Engines find that metadata through a catalog. Snowflake can manage Iceberg tables in your bucket, or read ones from a catalog like AWS Glue. Databricks can publish Delta tables with Iceberg metadata, served through Unity Catalog's Iceberg REST interface.
So a gold table of ten gigabytes is stored once, not twice. The writer commits a new metadata file, and the reader picks it up on its next lookup.

show.title: Storage for a 10 GB gold table

check.q: What does the Iceberg metadata tell a reading engine?
opts: Which Parquet files make up the table right now
Which users may see which columns
How to rewrite the table in its own format
check.why: Iceberg metadata lists the current data files. Access rules are not part of it, which is why governance has to be set separately on each platform.

work: Pick one gold table and trace which catalog and bucket path an external reader would use.
Measure how long a new commit takes to show up on the reading engine.

title: Where shared tables break

beats.say: Why does letting two engines write to one table corrupt it?

A commit works by swapping the pointer to the latest metadata file in the catalog. If two engines commit through different catalogs, each has its own pointer. Neither sees the other's change, so one silently overwrites the other and files get orphaned.
The catalog also hands out storage credentials, so it is the gatekeeper for the bucket. Pick one catalog as the system of record and connect the others to it.
Governance does not travel. A column mask in Unity Catalog means nothing to Snowflake, so a reader could see raw emails. Define the rule again on every platform that can read the data.

check.q: A column mask is set in Unity Catalog. Snowflake reads the same Iceberg table. What is true?
opts: Snowflake inherits the mask automatically
Snowflake ignores the mask unless you define its own policy
The table becomes unreadable in Snowflake
check.why: Iceberg carries data file lists, not access policies. Each platform must enforce its own rules, ideally generated from one definition.

work: Audit every table that has more than one engine able to commit to it.
Test a masked column from the second platform and confirm the mask exists there too.

title: Share it or copy it?

beats.say: Should you share one Iceberg table, or just copy the data?

Share when data is big and both teams need it fresh. You pay for storage once and avoid pipelines that break in the night. Copy when the reader needs heavy performance tuning, or strict isolation from the writer.

show.title: Choosing
items: Share: no copy pipelines to break
Copy: heavy tuning for the reader

beats.say: A design you can defend: the lakehouse engine writes bronze and silver. Gold is published as Iceberg. The warehouse reads it with no copy. Each platform enforces its own access policies, generated from one definition.

The tradeoff is coupling. Both platforms now depend on one catalog and one writer, so an outage or a metadata change there hits everyone. Budget for catalog availability and for policy generation, because those are the real cost, not the storage.

check.q: What is the main cost of sharing one Iceberg table across two platforms?
opts: Doubled storage bills
Coupling to one catalog and one writer, plus duplicated policy work
Loss of Parquet support
check.why: Storage drops because there is one copy. The new costs are dependence on a shared catalog and writer, and keeping access policies consistent on every platform.

work: Write down the one catalog and one writer for each shared table, and who is on call for them.
Generate access policies for both platforms from a single source definition and test them.

title: Making a library forget a reader

beats.say: How do you make a library forget a person, when it keeps a spare copy of everything? Let's find out.

show.sub: When it keeps spare copies of everything

beats.say: Say a reader asks to be erased. You cross out her name in the main book. But every night the library also saved old copies on a back shelf. Those copies still show her name. Crossing out is not the same as forgetting.

The clever fix is to never write her name in the books at all. Write only card number seventeen. One small locked notebook says seventeen is Asha. When she asks to be forgotten, tear out that one line. Every book still says seventeen, but seventeen now points to nobody.

check.q: Why is it smart to write only a card number in every book and keep the name in one notebook?
opts: The books become shorter to read
Erasing a person means changing one place, not every copy
It stops anyone from borrowing the books
check.why: The name lives in one spot. Remove it there and every other record holds a number that points to nobody.

work: List where a person's name or email is written in your data, and count the places.
Ask which one table could hold identity while all others use an id.

title: Why a delete does not erase

beats.say: You ran delete for one rider in your Delta table. So why is her data still readable?
Because a delete does not edit files. Delta writes a new table version, version 43, that skips the rider's rows. Version 42 and its old files stay on disk, so time travel can still show her.

So erasure takes three steps. One, find every copy: raw files, bronze, silver, gold, the warehouse, Kafka topics inside retention, exports and backups. Lineage is the map that lists them. Two, delete logically from each table.
Three, delete physically. On Delta, run vacuum once the retention window, seven days by default, has passed. On Iceberg, expire snapshots and remove orphan files. Only then are the bytes really gone.

show.title: Physical delete
items: Delta: vacuum after the retention window, seven days by default
Iceberg: expire snapshots, remove orphan files
Only then are the bytes gone

check.q: After a logical delete in Delta, why can time travel still show the rider?
opts: The delete failed silently
The old table version and its files remain until vacuumed
Time travel caches rows in memory
check.why: A delete writes a new version. Old files stay on disk until a physical cleanup such as vacuum removes them.

work: Write a runbook with the three steps: find copies, delete logically, delete physically.
Check your vacuum or snapshot expiry settings and note how long deleted data lingers.

title: Where erased data still hides

beats.say: You vacuumed the table, so is the rider gone? Not necessarily.

Vacuum only removes files older than the retention period, so a seven day window means seven more days of exposure. Shorten it and you break time travel and long running readers. Snowflake is similar: data leaves Time Travel, then Fail-safe, on its own schedules.

Copies hide elsewhere. Kafka topics keep the event until retention expires. Backups hold old snapshots. Exports sit in someone's bucket. Even derived tables, like a feature table or a model training set, can carry the rider. Without lineage you will miss one.
Tokenisation has a catch too. Joins work because the same input always gives the same token, but that also means anyone holding the token mapping can relink people. Guard that mapping.

show.title: Tokenisation catch
items: Same input gives the same token, so joins work
Whoever holds the mapping can relink people
Lock down and audit the mapping

check.q: You deleted a rider and ran vacuum straight away, but old files remain. What is the most likely reason?
opts: Vacuum ignores deleted rows
Files are younger than the retention period, so vacuum keeps them
Delta never removes files
check.why: Vacuum only deletes files older than the retention window, so the data lingers until that time passes.

work: Map every place a rider id could appear, including Kafka, backups and training sets.
Document how long each store keeps deleted data, then check it against your legal deadline.

title: Design so erasure costs one row

beats.say: Would you rather erase one row, or rewrite a petabyte? Your design decides.

show.sub: Design decides the cost of erasure

beats.say: Put personal data in one small table keyed by a surrogate id. Every other table holds only that id. Erasing a person becomes one row delete and one vacuum on a tiny table, not a rewrite of billions of event rows across every layer.

chip.text: Erase here, ids resolve to nobody

beats.say: The trade-offs. Masking and row policies cut who can see data, but they do not erase it. Tokenising in the pipeline means most tables never see the real value, at the cost of a lookup service to run and protect. Rewriting big tables to delete rows costs compute, so batch requests weekly, inside the legal deadline.

show.title: Trade-offs
items: Masking and row policies limit viewing, not existence
Tokenising: fewer tables hold real values, but you run a protected lookup
Big-table rewrites cost compute, so batch requests

beats.say: Choose the identity table early. Retrofitting it onto a lake full of raw emails is the expensive path, and old copies still need hunting.

check.q: Which design makes a right-to-be-forgotten request cheapest at scale?
opts: Column masking on every table
Personal data in one table, with a surrogate id everywhere else
Longer retention so deletes can be undone
check.why: Masking hides values but leaves them stored. Isolating identity in one table turns erasure into a tiny delete.

work: Propose a surrogate id and a single identity table for your next data model.
Batch erasure requests on a schedule that still meets the legal deadline.

title: Sorting notes with a pricey expert

beats.say: Imagine paying an expert by the word to sort a million cancellation notes every night. How do you keep the bill sane?

show.sub: an expert who charges by the word

beats.say: Riders type a reason when they cancel. Product wants those sorted into piles, like late driver, price, or changed mind. A language model can read each note and pick a pile. But it charges for every word it reads.
So you do three sensible things. Only hand it new notes. If two notes say the same thing, ask once and reuse the answer. And write on each note which expert and which instructions sorted it.

show.title: Three sensible habits
items: Same words? Ask once, reuse the answer
Stamp who sorted it, and with what instructions

check.q: Two thousand riders wrote exactly 'driver late'. What is the cheapest sensible approach?
opts: Send all two thousand to the model
Ask the model once and reuse the answer
Skip those rows entirely
check.why: Identical text gets an identical answer, so one call can serve every copy. That cuts cost without losing any rows.

work: Find one place where you pay per call and count how many inputs are duplicates.
Write down who or what produced each derived label in your tables.

title: Rows times tokens: controlling the bill

beats.say: A million rows, a hundred tokens each. What does that cost every night?
That is one hundred million input tokens. A token is a small chunk of text, roughly three quarters of a word. Cost is rows times tokens, so you shrink both.

First, process only new or changed rows, like any incremental model. If fifty thousand rows are new, you skip ninety five percent of the work. Second, cache by input. Normalise the text, hash it, and call the model once per distinct value. Driver late may appear ten thousand times and cost one call.
Third, use the smallest model that passes your evaluation. Fourth, count the calls before making any. If the count is over budget, stop and alert.

check.q: Why count the calls before making any?
opts: To make the model answer faster
To stop and alert if the run would blow the budget
To pick the category list
check.why: Spend is irreversible once calls are made. A pre-run count lets you fail early, before money is spent.

work: Add a dry-run step that counts distinct uncached inputs and compares it to a limit.
Hash normalised text (trim, lowercase) and keep a cache table of text hash to label.

title: Making model output safe to trust

beats.say: Last month the same reason got two different labels. Could you tell which run did it?
Store the prompt version and model name on every output row. Then you know which rows came from which version, and you re-run only when the improvement is worth the cost.

Model replies are free text, and free text breaks tables. Ask for one value from a closed list of categories, including unknown, and validate on return. Anything off the list becomes unknown, never a new category.

Riders also type names and phone numbers. Mask them before the text leaves your platform. Finally, hand label a few hundred rows and measure accuracy before the first full run and after every prompt change.

show.title: Before and after every change
items: Mask names and phone numbers first
Hand label a few hundred rows
Measure accuracy before the first run

check.q: The model returns a category not on your list. What should the pipeline do?
opts: Add it to the table as a new category
Map it to unknown and keep the row
Retry until it matches, with no limit
check.why: A closed list keeps downstream tables stable. Unknown is an honest label and unlimited retries would break your budget.

work: Add prompt_version and model_name columns to every model-labelled table.
Build a hand-labelled test set of a few hundred rows and run it on each prompt change.
Add a masking step for phone numbers and names before any external call.

title: Batch endpoints and when to skip the model

beats.say: Does this job need an answer in one second, or by morning?

A nightly job can wait. So use a provider batch endpoint. You submit a large set of requests, the provider works through them asynchronously, and you collect results later. You trade latency for a usually lower price and fewer rate limit headaches.

The warehouse SQL function is the fastest way to try an idea. But it hides the calls, so caching, budgets and prompt versions are harder to control. Once it matters, move the call into a pipeline step you own.

show.title: SQL function trade-off
items: Harder to cache, budget and version
Own the step once it matters

beats.say: And ask if you need a model at all. If keywords catch most reasons, send only the leftovers to the model. With labelled rows from your evaluation, a small trained classifier may be cheaper still.

check.q: A nightly classification job has no deadline within the night. What is the best fit?
opts: A per-row SQL model call inside every query
A provider batch endpoint with cached, deduplicated inputs
A live endpoint called once per rider click
check.why: Work that can wait gains from asynchronous batch processing, and deduplication cuts volume further. Live calls pay for latency you do not need.

work: Check whether your model calls really need real-time answers; move the rest to a batch endpoint.
Measure how many rows simple rules could label, and send only the remainder to the model.
Keep the labelled evaluation set so you can compare a smaller model or classifier later.

title: The notebook by the warehouse door

beats.say: How can a pile of files behave like a real database table? Picture a warehouse full of boxes, and a notebook by the door.
Nobody trusts the shelves. They trust the notebook. Each line says box three added, or box one thrown out. To know what is in the warehouse today, read the notebook from the top.
Boxes are only crossed out, never burned. So you can read the notebook up to last Tuesday and see what was there then. Now and then someone writes a summary page, so you skip the early pages.

show.title: Why it works
items: Read to any earlier line for the past

check.q: In the warehouse analogy, what tells you what the table contains today?
opts: The boxes on the shelves
The notebook read from the top
The newest box only
check.why: Shelves may hold crossed-out boxes. The notebook, the log, says which files count right now.

work: Open a Delta table folder and look at the _delta_log files.
Read one commit JSON and find its add and remove lines.

title: Two writers, one commit number

beats.say: Two jobs write to the same table at the same moment. Who wins?
Each writer first saves its Parquet data files. Then it tries to create the next numbered file in the log, say commit eleven. Only one writer can create that number. The other is refused.
The loser checks whether the winner touched the same files. If not, it retries as commit twelve. If they clash, it fails. That is optimistic concurrency: assume no clash, then check afterward.
Readers replay the log, adds minus removes. A checkpoint every ten commits saves that state, so a reader loads one checkpoint and a few small files, not thousands.

check.q: A writer is refused commit eleven because another writer got it first. What happens next?
opts: It overwrites commit eleven
It checks for conflicts, then retries as twelve or fails
It waits for a lock to be released
check.why: Only one writer can create a given number. The loser compares the winner's changes with its own and either retries on top or fails.

work: Run two concurrent writes to a test table and read the commit files.
Find the checkpoint file and note which commit it covers.

title: Past versions and strict schemas

beats.say: Can you query a table as it was last week, even after someone deleted half of it?

Yes. A delete never erases a file. It writes a commit that marks the file removed. The old file stays on disk, so version twelve is just the log replayed up to commit twelve. Use VERSION AS OF or TIMESTAMP AS OF.

show.title: Time travel
show.text:
SELECT count(*) FROM trips VERSION AS OF 12;
DESCRIBE HISTORY trips;
show.note: Replay the log only up to commit 12

beats.say: Schema enforcement works at write time. If the columns do not match the table, the write is rejected. A typo upstream becomes a failed job, not a silent new column. Adding columns is opt in, with the merge schema option.

check.q: An upstream job renames a column by mistake and writes to a Delta table with default settings. What happens?
opts: A new column is added silently
The write is rejected
The old column is dropped
check.why: Enforcement is the default. Schema evolution, such as merge schema, must be switched on deliberately.

work: Run DESCRIBE HISTORY on a key table and read the versions.
Check which pipelines set merge schema and ask if they need it.

title: Small files, optimize and vacuum

beats.say: Why does a Delta table get slower every week, and why can vacuum break time travel?

Streaming writes create many tiny files, and each one costs a metadata lookup and an open. OPTIMIZE rewrites them into fewer large files. Z order also sorts rows so similar values share files, and then min and max statistics let readers skip most files.
Optimize leaves the old files behind, marked removed. VACUUM deletes them for real, once they are older than the retention period. The default is seven days.

show.title: Vacuum rules
items: Deletes files no live version needs

beats.say: The catch: after vacuum runs, time travel beyond that point is gone. A long running reader, or a stream that has fallen behind, can also fail when its files vanish.

check.q: You run OPTIMIZE and storage use does not drop. Why?
opts: Optimize failed silently
The old files are still kept until VACUUM removes them
Z order increases file size
check.why: Optimize only marks the small files as removed in the log. They stay on disk for time travel until vacuum deletes them.

work: Check the file count and average file size of your busiest table.
Confirm your vacuum retention is longer than your slowest stream or job.

title: Deletion vectors and the change feed

beats.say: Delete one row from a one gigabyte file. Do you really rewrite the whole gigabyte?

By default, yes. That is copy on write. With deletion vectors, Delta writes a tiny side file that marks the row as gone, and readers skip it. That is merge on read: cheap writes, slightly costlier reads until the next rewrite.
Change Data Feed goes further. It exposes row level inserts, updates and deletes between two versions, so a downstream job reads only what changed, not the whole table.
One gotcha: the feed only records changes made after you switch it on. It cannot rebuild earlier history.

check.q: What do deletion vectors trade away to make deletes cheap?
opts: Atomicity of the commit
Slightly slower reads until files are rewritten
The ability to time travel
check.why: Readers must apply the side file to skip deleted rows. This is merge on read, so reads cost a little more until a rewrite folds the deletes in.

work: List your tables with frequent small deletes and test deletion vectors on one.
Enable Change Data Feed on a source table before building its downstream job.

title: Choosing a layout for a new table

beats.say: You are designing a new two terabyte trips table. Do you partition it by date?

Probably not. Partitions are fixed at creation. Pick a poor column and you get thousands of tiny folders, and changing it means rewriting everything. Z order helps, but it is not incremental, so each run rewrites more.
Liquid clustering is the current advice. Name your filter columns with CLUSTER BY. It clusters incrementally, and you can change those columns later without rewriting the table.
Keep date partitions only when the table is huge and every query filters by date. And budget for upkeep: optimize and vacuum are compute you pay for, and long retention is storage you pay for.

show.title: Decide
items: Partition: huge and always by date

check.q: Your filter columns may change as usage evolves. Which layout copes best?
opts: Partition by the first filter column
Z order on the current columns
Liquid clustering
check.why: Liquid clustering lets you change clustering columns later without rewriting the whole table. Partitions are fixed, and Z order is not incremental.

work: Review your partitioned tables and find any with tiny partitions.
Pilot liquid clustering on one new table and compare scan times.

title: When many writers fight over one table

beats.say: Fifty jobs all update the same Delta table. Does it scale?
Not well. Optimistic concurrency assumes clashes are rare. When many writers touch the same files, losers retry or fail, and all that wasted work costs compute.

Reduce clashes by making writers touch different files, through clustering or partitions that match each job. Funnel small writes into fewer, larger commits. Deletion vectors also shrink what an update touches.

show.title: Reduce clashes
items: Give each writer its own files

beats.say: Also watch commit frequency. A commit every second is eighty six thousand log files a day, plus piles of tiny data files. A micro batch every minute is often enough.

check.q: Many jobs keep failing with conflicts on one table. What is the best first fix?
opts: Add more retries
Make jobs write to disjoint files and batch their commits
Raise the vacuum retention
check.why: Conflicts occur when writers touch the same files. Separating them and committing less often cuts the clashes. More retries only burns compute.

work: Check your conflict and retry rates on the busiest table.
Raise streaming trigger intervals where freshness allows.

title: A rented kitchen or your own

beats.say: Why do companies pay for Snowflake or Databricks instead of running their own data engine?
Think of a restaurant. Snowflake is a fully run kitchen: you hand over ingredients and recipes, and staff handle the ovens, cleaning and storage. You pay for every minute the ovens are on.
Databricks is a kitchen built in your own building, on your own shelves. You get more control and more kinds of cooking, like Python and machine learning, but you choose more settings.
Running your own engine on open tables is a third choice: cheapest at large scale, but you hire the kitchen staff yourself.

show.title: Three choices
items: Open engine: you run it all

check.q: What is the main trade when you run an open engine yourself instead of a managed platform?
opts: You lose SQL support
You save the vendor bill but must operate everything
Your data must leave the cloud
check.why: Open engines avoid the platform fee, but your team runs the engine, catalog, compaction and upgrades.

work: Write down who in your company would operate an open engine if you chose one.
List the workloads that are pure SQL and the ones that need Python or ML.

title: Pruning and micro-partitions

beats.say: Snowflake has no indexes. So how does it skip most of a billion row table?
Each table is split into micro-partitions of about fifty to five hundred megabytes. For every one, Snowflake records the minimum and maximum of each column.
A query for day eight checks that metadata first. Parts one and two cannot hold day eight, so they are never read. Only part three is scanned.
This works when data arrives in the order you filter by, like events by date. When it does not, a clustering key re-sorts the data in the background, and you pay credits for it.

check.q: Why can Snowflake skip micro-partitions for a date filter on time-ordered data?
opts: It builds an index on every column
Each part records the min and max of its columns
It caches every table in memory
check.why: Pruning compares the filter with stored min and max values and skips parts that cannot match.

work: Open a slow query profile and compare partitions scanned with partitions total.
Check whether your largest table is loaded in the order it is filtered.

title: Warehouses, credits and caches

beats.say: Is a bigger Snowflake warehouse more expensive? Often not. Here is why.
Each size step doubles the power and doubles the credits per hour. Billing is per second, with a one minute minimum. If a query runs twice as fast on the next size, it costs about the same.

Caches cut the bill further. The result cache returns an identical query on unchanged data for a day, with no warehouse running. Metadata answers counts and min and max. The warehouse disk keeps data it read, until it suspends.
So set auto suspend to a few minutes: too short loses the warm cache, too long pays for idle time.

chip.text: A few minutes is a good start

check.q: A query takes 8 minutes on Medium and 4 on Large. Which costs more?
opts: Large, because it is bigger
About the same, since Large uses twice the credits for half the time
Medium, because of the one minute minimum
check.why: Each size doubles credits per hour; halving the run time keeps the cost roughly equal.

work: Measure one heavy job on two warehouse sizes and compare credits.
Check auto suspend on every BI warehouse.

title: Clustering versus search optimization

beats.say: Your query looks for one customer among billions of rows, and pruning does nothing. What now?
A clustering key re-sorts data so similar values sit together. It helps range filters, such as a date or region, on very large tables with stable filters.

The search optimization service builds a hidden lookup structure instead. It suits equality on high cardinality ids, substring search and fields inside variant columns, where no single sort order helps.
Both bill storage and serverless credits in the background. Measure partitions scanned before and after, and remove what does not pay.

check.q: Which tool suits finding a few rows by a high cardinality id on time ordered data?
opts: A larger warehouse
The search optimization service
A multi-cluster warehouse
check.why: A time order cannot prune id lookups; search optimization builds a lookup structure for them.

work: Find tables with automatic clustering and check their monthly credits.
List point-lookup queries that scan most partitions.

title: Time Travel, clones and hidden storage

beats.say: A clone of a ten terabyte table is created in seconds and costs nothing. Then the bill grows anyway. Why?
Micro-partitions are never changed in place. An update writes new parts. A clone copies only metadata, so both tables point at the same parts until either side changes.

Old parts are kept for Time Travel, one day by default and up to ninety on Enterprise, then seven more days of Fail safe for permanent tables. A table with heavy updates can hold many times its live size.
Use transient tables for staging, which skip Fail safe, and keep long Time Travel only where you need it.

check.q: Why can a heavily updated Snowflake table cost far more storage than its live size?
opts: Clones always copy data
Old micro-partitions are kept for Time Travel and Fail safe
Snowflake stores data uncompressed
check.why: Updates write new parts; old ones stay for the retention periods and are billed.

work: Query table storage metrics for your busiest tables.
Make staging tables transient.

title: Photon, deletion vectors and liquid clustering

beats.say: Three Databricks features are often confused. Each works at a different layer.
Photon is the engine. A C plus plus vectorised engine runs SQL and DataFrame operators on column batches. It is on by default in SQL warehouses and serverless, and costs more on classic clusters.
Deletion vectors change writes. Deleting ten rows records their positions in a small side file instead of rewriting a whole Parquet file. Readers skip those rows.

Liquid clustering changes layout. Cluster by your filter columns replaces partitions and Z order, clusters incrementally, and lets you change keys without a rewrite. All three are generally available.

check.q: A team says Photon will fix slow filters on an unclustered table. What is wrong?
opts: Photon only works on Snowflake
Photon speeds execution but does not change which files are read
Photon disables liquid clustering
check.why: Photon is the engine; skipping files depends on layout such as liquid clustering.

work: Check which of your jobs pay for Photon but run mostly Python UDFs.
Move one partitioned table to liquid clustering on its filter columns.

title: Unity Catalog and serverless

beats.say: Who controls access, and who pays for the machines, in Databricks?

Unity Catalog is one governance layer across workspaces: three level names, grants, row filters, column masks, lineage and storage credentials, so no user holds bucket keys. It is generally available and open source.

Classic compute runs in your cloud account: you pick instances and networking, and pay DBUs plus virtual machines. Serverless runs in the vendor account, starts in seconds, and its DBU price includes the machines, with less control.

check.q: What do you give up by moving a job from classic to serverless compute?
opts: Unity Catalog permissions
Some control over instance types and network paths
Delta Lake support
check.why: Serverless runs in the vendor account with managed machines, so you trade some control for fast starts and no sizing.

work: List the jobs that need special hardware or network paths.
Move one scheduled job to serverless and compare its cost.

title: Snowflake, Databricks or open tables

beats.say: The board asks: Snowflake, Databricks, or Iceberg on Trino? Answer with workloads, not brands.
SQL analytics and dashboards with a small platform team point to Snowflake. Python, Spark, streaming and machine learning on data in your own bucket point to Databricks.
Many engines, strict open format rules, or petabyte costs with a strong platform team point to Iceberg with a REST catalog and Trino. You trade the vendor bill for running everything yourself.
Many companies combine them: Databricks writes, gold tables are published as Iceberg, and Snowflake reads them without a copy. Always name one writer per table.

check.q: Two platforms read one Iceberg table. What rule prevents corruption?
opts: Both engines commit through their own catalogs
Exactly one engine writes, through one catalog of record
Copy the table into each platform
check.why: One writer and one catalog of record keep commits consistent; others only read.

work: Write a one page comparison for your main workloads.
Name the single writer for every shared table.
